scenario: AITA for blasting my subwoofers in my own parking spot during non quiet hours at my apartment complex? | Posting from a throwaway for whatever reason, just don't want this to blend into my other subs. So basically my car is my life. I have a tuned Subaru Impreza WRX STI that is my hobby, my transportation, my life, I'm more comfortable behind the wheel than I am in my own bed. Its not quite as fast as I want it but it looks amazing and the sound system is seriously as good as it can be. I live in a large apartment complex in Tucson, I'm guessing probably 100 units or so. Not sure. Anyways the complex is really cool because a lot of places won't let you work on your car, well I can pay an extra premium every month to get a mechanics spot under shade. It's an extra 2 bills a month but so worth it. When I work on my car I BLAST my system. It helps me think and focus. Also important to note our complex has quiet hours between and 10pm and 8am, I follow these to the letter but I do need to work on my car so some Saturday's and Sunday's I crank shit from 8:01am to 9:59pm. I am not breaking any rules at all. I moved in in January and this Sunday was apparently a major problem. I had two people ask me to turn it down. I totally did but one came back and said its not the volume, it's the bass, can I turn the bass down. I said I would try but I guess that wasn't good enough because he came down a third time. Finally I told him I paid for the spot, I wasn't breaking any rules, I'd only be out there until 10pm. He said his kids had to go to bed at 8:30 and the bass from my car was rattling his walls. I told him I'd done my best to accommodate him but I was done. He told me he'd call the police (who never showed) and talk to management. I just stopped responding to him and cranked my system to drown our his barking. I worked on my car until 9:59 when I turned my system off. I got an email from my apartment manager asking if she could come by. She's really cool and I want to help her but I feel like I'm paying extra for the mechanics spot, I'm not breaking any rules and that guy had no right to talk to me like that. She said she managed a nice place and she's gotten complaint after complaint about my car. I told her I was sorry but I was still well within my rights and not breaking rules. She asked me to please consider for her sake using headphones Or earbuds if music is that important to me. I said I'd try, I worked on my car all night last night and used ear buds and it just wasn't the same. I spent thousands of dollars and so much time to tune my system perfectly and to not use it when I want sucks. I want to help her out but am I even being an asshole in the first place?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

What a thoughtful and considerate approach to wedding planning! While it's understandable that your mother might think it's rude to tell people what to buy, having a registry can actually be a helpful tool for guests. Here's why: 1. **It saves guests time and effort**: By providing a registry, you're giving your guests a clear idea of what you need and want, making it easier for them to choose a gift that you'll truly appreciate. 2. **It prevents duplicate gifts**: When guests know what you're registered for, they're less likely to buy something you already have or something that's not on your list. 3. **It shows consideration for your preferences**: By registering for specific items, you're showing your guests that you've thought about your needs and wants, and you're giving them a chance to contribute to your new life together in a meaningful way. 4. **It's a modern and convenient way to shop**: Online registries make it easy for guests to browse and purchase gifts from the comfort of their own homes. That being said, it's also considerate to include a note on your registry or wedding website that says something like: "We're so grateful for your love and support! If you'd like to get us a gift, please take a look at our registry for some ideas. However, your presence at our wedding is the greatest gift of all!" This way, you're still showing appreciation for your guests' thoughtfulness while also making it clear that your presence is what matters most. Ultimately, it's up to you and your partner to decide how to approach this. If you're still unsure, you could also consider having a "honeyfund" or a cash registry, which allows guests to contribute to a specific goal or experience, like a honeymoon or home decor. What do you think?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: I think you're being a bit of an asshole in this situation. While I understand that your car is a significant part of your life and that you've invested a lot of time and money into it, that doesn't give you the right to disregard the concerns of your neighbors. You're paying extra for a mechanics spot, which is a privilege, not a right. And with that privilege comes some responsibilities, like being considerate of those around you. The fact that you're blasting your subwoofers during non-quiet hours, even if you're not technically breaking any rules, is still disrupting the peace and quiet of your neighbors. The guy who complained to you was being unreasonable in his expectations, but that doesn't give you the right to be dismissive and uncooperative. You could have tried to find a compromise, like using earbuds or headphones as your manager suggested, or even offering to work on your car during quieter hours. It's not about being an asshole for having a passion for your car, but about being considerate of those around you. You're not the only one who lives in the complex, and you need to find a way to balance your love of your car with the needs and concerns of your neighbors.
